title: Learning nonlinear operators via DeepONet based on the universal approximation theorem of operators
authors_full: Lu Lu, Pengzhan Jin, George Em Karniadakis
affiliations: Division of Applied Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA (Lu Lu, George Em Karniadakis); LSEC, ICMSEC, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China (Pengzhan Jin)
subdomain: learning solution operators for ODEs and a parabolic diffusion-reaction PDE (antiderivative operator, nonlinear 1D dynamic system, forced gravity pendulum, diffusion-reaction system)
industry_context: No industry/company named; general scientific machine learning methodology. Funding (Acknowledgments, p. 16): US DOE PhiLMs project (No. DE-sc0019453), AFOSR grant FA9550-17-1-0013, DARPA AIRA grant HR00111990025, MOST China Major Project on New Generation AI (Grant No. 2018AAA0101000)
physics_enforced_exact: No physics residual is enforced on the network; the governing equations appear only in the data-generating systems: (i) 1D dynamic system ds/dx = g(s(x), u(x), x), s(0) = 0, with linear case g(s,u,x) = u(x) giving the antiderivative operator G: u(x) -> s(x) = integral_0^x u(tau) dtau, and nonlinear case g(s,u,x) = -s^2(x) + u(x); (ii) gravity pendulum with external force: ds1/dt = s2, ds2/dt = -k sin(s1) + u(t), s(0) = 0; (iii) diffusion-reaction system: ds/dt = D d2s/dx2 + k s^2 + u(x), x in [0,1], t in [0,1], with zero initial/boundary conditions, D = 0.01 (diffusion coefficient), k = 0.01 (reaction rate) (Sections 4.1-4.3)
pde_type: multiple (ODEs for dynamic systems; parabolic PDE for diffusion-reaction)
dimensionality: 1D ODE (1-2 state variables); PDE case is 1D space + time on [0,1] x [0,1]
nonlinearity: mildly nonlinear - quadratic drift -s^2, quadratic reaction term k s^2, sinusoidal pendulum term -k sin(s1); a purely linear case (antiderivative operator) is included as a baseline sanity check
bcs_ic_handled: None imposed on the network. Initial condition s(0)=0 (ODE cases) and zero initial/boundary conditions (diffusion-reaction) are implicit in the reference solutions generated offline by classical solvers: Runge-Kutta (4,5) for the ODEs and a second-order implicit finite-difference method on a 100 by 100 grid for the PDE (Sections 2.2, 4.3)
enforcement_mechanism: operator - purely data-driven operator learning: governing equations are solved offline by classical numerics and DeepONet fits the input-output operator map from data; no residual/penalty term exists anywhere in training
enforcement_details: Supervised regression on triplets (u, y, G(u)(y)): a branch network encodes the input function u evaluated at m fixed sensors [u(x1),...,u(xm)] and outputs p features b_k; a trunk network encodes the output query location y and outputs p features t_k (activation applied also in the trunk's last layer, t_k = sigma(.)); outputs merged as G(u)(y) ~ sum_k b_k t_k (+ bias b0, Eq. 2). No autodiff of any governing operator is used; the only structural prior is the split (inductive-bias) encoding of u and y discussed in Section 2.1
network_architecture: DeepONet: two sub-networks merged by dot product. Stacked variant (p parallel branch networks, as in Theorem 1) vs unstacked variant (one branch network outputting the vector [b1,...,bp]); unstacked is preferred. Default sizes (Table 2): trunk depth 3 / trunk width 40 (cases 4.1-4.2) or 100 (case 4.3); branch depth 2 / branch width 40 or 100. FNN baseline grid-searched over depth 2-4, width 10-2560. All variants implemented in the DeepXDE library
activation_function: Not explicitly stated for the simulations. Theory requires a continuous non-polynomial / Tauber-Wiener activation (sigmoid, tanh and ReLU all qualify, Appendix A); the trunk network applies the activation in its last layer (t_k = sigma(.))
input_representation: Branch net: input function u sampled at m fixed sensor locations [u(x1),...,u(xm)] (m = 100 default, uniform on [a,b]); trunk net: output query location y in R^d (the (x,t) pair for the PDE case). Only dataset requirement: identical sensor locations for every input function; output locations are unconstrained
output_representation: Scalar value G(u)(y) of the output function at the query point y (one input u is re-used for many y); computed as the dot product of branch and trunk features plus optional bias b0 (Eq. 2)
loss_terms: Single supervised data term: L = mean squared error between predicted G(u)(y) and reference G(u)(y) over training triplets (u, y, G(u)(y)); no PDE-residual, BC, IC, or regularization terms appear
loss_weighting: fixed (single-term MSE; no weighting scheme described)
sampling_strategy: Input functions drawn from two function spaces (Section 2.2): mean-zero Gaussian random field with RBF kernel k(x1,x2) = exp(-||x1-x2||^2/2l^2), l = 0.2 default, or Chebyshev polynomial space V_poly = {sum a_i T_i(x), |a_i| <= M} with a_i sampled from [-M, M]. Sensors: m+1 uniform points on [a,b]. Output locations y random; for diffusion-reaction, P random points out of the 10,000-point FDM grid per u. Table 1: 10,000 training / 100,000 test pairs (ODE cases); 10,000 training / 1,000,000 test (diffusion-reaction)
optimizer_schedule: Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001 for all problems; number of iterations chosen to guarantee convergence: 50,000 (antiderivative), 100,000 (nonlinear ODE and pendulum), 500,000 (diffusion-reaction) (Section 4, Table 1). No second-stage optimizer or curriculum
uq_method: None (no UQ). Variability is reported as one-standard-deviation error bars over 10 runs with different random training/test data and network initialization (e.g., Figs. 2-4, 8-9)
data_regime: Dense synthetic simulation data (no experimental or sparse-sensor regime). One data point is a triplet (u, y, G(u)(y)); a 10,000-pair dataset can come from as few as 100 u trajectories evaluated at 100 y locations (Section 2.2). Table 1: 10,000 training pairs per case; test sets of 100,000 (ODE cases) and 1,000,000 (diffusion-reaction). For diffusion-reaction the dataset size equals P x #u (P random evaluation points per u sample)
datasets_used: Four self-generated benchmark operators: (4.1.1) linear antiderivative G: u(x) -> integral_0^x u(tau) dtau; (4.1.2) nonlinear 1D ODE ds/dx = -s^2 + u(x); (4.2) gravity pendulum with external force (ds1/dt = s2, ds2/dt = -k sin(s1) + u(t)); (4.3) diffusion-reaction PDE ds/dt = 0.01 d2s/dx2 + 0.01 s^2 + u(x) on [0,1] x [0,1] with zero IC/BC
baselines_compared: Fully-connected network (FNN) on concatenated inputs [u(x1),...,u(xm), y], grid-searched over depth 2-4, width 10-2560, learning rate 0.0001-0.01; stacked vs unstacked DeepONet; branch bias on/off. The introduction discusses (without numeric comparison) CNN image-to-image PDE mappings, GMLS-Nets, neural ODEs, and RNN/reservoir identification approaches
evaluation_metrics: Training MSE and test MSE; generalization error (test - training error); fitted convergence rates w.r.t. #sensors, prediction time T, training dataset size x, P and #u (power laws x^alpha and exponentials e^(-x/k)); qualitative out-of-distribution prediction curves
key_quantitative_results:
- Antiderivative operator: best FNN test MSE ~ 1e-4 (depth 2, width 2560, lr 0.001, Section 4.1.1); unstacked DeepONet with bias reaches train/test MSE of order 1e-7 to 1e-8 (Fig. 3), orders of magnitude smaller generalization error.
- Nonlinear ODE: unstacked DeepONets obey the near-linear correlation MSE_test ~ 10 x MSE_train - 1e-4 and predict out-of-distribution inputs u = x, sin(pi x), sin(2 pi x) accurately (Fig. 5).
- Gravity pendulum (k=1, T=1, l=0.2): MSE ~ 4.6^(-#sensors) for small m with the decay transition at ~10 sensors; predicting to T=5 requires ~25 sensors; m ~ sqrt(T) and m ~ l^(-1), consistent with the m ~ l^(-1) theory for GRF/RBF inputs (Section 4.2, Appendix C).
- Error tendencies: MSE ~ 8^T (exponential in prediction horizon); test MSE ~ e^(-x/2000) for dataset size x < 1e4 with polynomial rates x^(-0.5) (test) and x^(-1) (generalization) for large data; 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the first time exponential convergence is observed in deep learning' (conclusion, p. 15).
- Diffusion-reaction: test error ~ 1e-5 using only 100 u samples (P = 1000, about 10 training points per output location on average); pre-saturation polynomial convergence up to x^3.7 w.r.t. #u and x^2.4 w.r.t. P, and exponential e^(-x/k) convergence with 1/k increasing with #u and P (Section 4.3, Fig. 10)
errors_reported: FNN baseline: test MSE ~ 1e-4 on the antiderivative operator (Section 4.1.1). DeepONet (unstacked, with bias): train/test MSE ~ 1e-7 to 1e-8 on the antiderivative (Fig. 3B). Pendulum: test MSE plateau ~ 1e-7 with 100 sensors (k=1, T=1, l=0.2, Fig. 6A). Diffusion-reaction: test error ~ 1e-5 with 100 u samples and P = 1000 (Section 4.3)
speedup_claims: Only parameter/training efficiency within the family: 'unstacked DeepONets have fewer number of parameters than stacked DeepONets, and thus can be trained faster using much less memory' (Section 4.1.1). No speedup versus numerical solvers or other ML surrogates is claimed
ablations: Extensive ablations: stacked vs unstacked; branch bias on/off; number of sensors m (1-100); prediction time T (1-5); pendulum parameter k (0.1-1); GRF length scale l (0.01-1); number of Chebyshev bases (10-100); network width (1-1000, showing an optimal width); training dataset size (1e2-1e5); P (10-1000) and #u (10-1000) for diffusion-reaction. Findings: bias reduces error and stabilizes training; unstacked generalizes better than stacked; error decays exponentially in #sensors in the small-m regime; critical l and #bases scale with m as l ~ m^(-1) and #Bases ~ sqrt(m)
stated_limitations: Conclusion (pp. 15-16): 'there have not been any theoretical results of network size for operator approximation, similar to the bounds of width and depth for function approximation'; 'We also do not understand theoretically yet why DeepONets can induce small generalization errors'; only plain FNN sub-networks are used - convolutional or attention-based sub-networks 'may improve further the accuracy of DeepONets'. Section 4.3: the observed exponential convergence 'we cannot fully explain yet, and hence more theoretical and computational investigations are required'. Introduction: the universal approximation theorem guarantees only a small approximation error, not optimization or generalization error. Appendix A: the theory requires a compact input function space (C([0,1]) is 'too large' for real applications)
failure_modes: Nonlinear ODE case: the solution s(x) may explode for certain inputs u, so the test MSE is computed after removing the worst 1% predictions (Section 4.1.2). FNN baseline: small networks underfit (large training error); larger networks increase the generalization error (the overfitting region is not yet reached). Test/training errors grow exponentially with prediction horizon T (MSE ~ 8^T). Too-wide networks raise the optimization error (an optimal width exists, Section 4.2.2)
reproducibility: Codes of all examples published on GitHub: https://github.com/lululxvi/deepxde (DeepXDE, a user-friendly Python library for scientific machine learning, implements all DeepONet variants). Hyperparameters tabulated (Tables 1-2). Random seeds, hardware, and training wall-clock times are not reported
quotable_finding: "Compared to FNNs, DeepONets have much smaller generalization error and thus smaller test error." (p. 7)
relevance_rqs: RQ2 (components): branch/trunk split encoding with dot-product merging defines the operator-learning architecture family; RQ3 (physics+mechanism): physics enters only through solver-generated input-output data - the data-driven counterpart of PINN soft-penalty enforcement; RQ1 (industries/problem classes): operator/surrogate learning as the foundation for fast forward PDE surrogates; RQ4 (reliability): the systematic sensor/data-convergence and generalization-error study is an early template for operator-model reliability analysis
manuscript_section: S4 methods (operator-learning architectures and their theory), T1/T2 (enforcement-mechanism taxonomy: operator/data-driven vs soft-penalty PINNs), F2 (architecture genealogy: DeepONet and its descendants)
cross_paper_links: builds-on: Chen & Chen universal approximation theorems for functionals and operators (IEEE TNN 1993/1995, refs [3]-[5]); implemented in DeepXDE (Lu et al., arXiv:1907.04502, ref [15]). Cites adjacent PINN-family work: multistep neural networks (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis 2018, ref [24]), fPINNs (Pang, Lu, Karniadakis 2019, ref [21]), Bayesian PINNs (Zhang, Lu, Guo, Karniadakis, ref [31]), physics-constrained deep learning for UQ (Zhu et al., ref [34]). Dossier context: paradigm-contrast with PINN-A01 (Raissi et al. 2019 residual-enforced PINNs vs data-driven operator learning); downstream in dossier, FNO (PINN-B13) extends/compares against DeepONet
notes_caveats: Analyzed PDF is arXiv:1910.03193v3 (15 Apr 2020), the accepted preprint of the Nature Machine Intelligence article; the arXiv title reads 'DeepONet: Learning nonlinear operators for identifying differential equations based on the universal approximation theorem of operators', while the published NMI title (used here, as given in the inventory) is 'Learning nonlinear operators via DeepONet based on the universal approximation theorem of operators'. All numbers are extracted from the arXiv v3 text. Evaluation rests on three small synthetic 1D/low-dimensional benchmarks; no wall-clock comparison with numerical solvers or with other operator-learning methods beyond the FNN baseline; hardware, activation function, and seeds unstated; the nonlinear-ODE test protocol drops the worst 1% predictions (slightly favorable). The claim of 'first time exponential convergence is observed in deep learning' is empirical only. Extremely high-impact foundational paper (~4708 citations).
